primary_issue: Severe overexposure/clipped whites: the frame is essentially washed out, so the oil stream, glass, and liquid surface are not readable.
issues: Exposure is heavily blown out across all sampled frames (0006/0024/0048), destroying midtone/shadow detail and color.
Intended effect (viscous oil stream into a glass) is not visually identifiable; no clear stream thickness/taper, no surface contact point, no fill level read.
Glass container is only hinted by faint vertical edges; rim, curvature, thickness, base, and refraction are not visible.
No visible ripples, meniscus, or bubbles—key interaction cues are missing or lost to clipping.
No apparent caustics/refractive light patterns; transparency/light-transport look is not achieved.
Only 3 frames are present in the output directory, so animation/fill-rate/temporal behavior cannot be properly evaluated.
suggestions: Reduce exposure substantially (e.g., -2 to -4 stops) and/or reduce light intensities by ~5–20× until the glass silhouette and oil color are readable.
Avoid a pure-white background/overpowering backlight; introduce controlled rim lighting and a slightly darker background to separate the stream and glass edges.
Ensure the oil material has visible absorption/tint (amber-gold) so it reads against the background; make sure transmission/refraction highlights are not clipping.
Add/adjust lighting to create specular rims on the glass (edge highlights) and visible refractive distortion through the cylinder.
Verify the simulation mesh is actually visible in render (not hidden/fully transparent) and that the stream intersects the glass opening at the intended height.
Render the full frame range (1–48) so temporal criteria (continuous pour, rising level, ripple damping, occasional bubbles) can be judged.
vision_assessment: All three sampled frames appear nearly white with extreme highlight clipping. The only discernible shapes are two very faint vertical lines suggesting where a glass might be, but the vessel does not read as clear glass (rim/base/refraction are not visible). There is no clearly visible olive-oil stream entering the glass, no contact point on a liquid surface, and no surface ripples or bubbles. The lack of contrast and blown-out exposure prevents evaluation of the intended viscous pour behavior and product-shot lighting look.
